_review: TODO-REVIEW: All checklist items must be reviewed by a qualified Lagos property lawyer and registered surveyor before publication.

categories.title: Title and Ownership Documents
categories.note: TODO-REVIEW: Document hierarchy and authenticity checks should be confirmed against current Lagos State Land Bureau practice.

items.task: Obtain the original Certificate of Occupancy (C of O) or Deed of Assignment and inspect it in person.
items.why: Photocopies can be forged. The original should bear the Land Registry seal and registration number.

items.task: Confirm the title document is registered at the Lagos State Land Registry (Alausa).
items.why: An unregistered deed provides weak legal protection.

items.task: Trace the chain of title back to the root (ideally a C of O) and check for any gaps or unexplained changes in ownership.
items.why: Gaps in the chain may indicate a fraudulent transfer at some point in the history.

items.task: Check that Governor's Consent was obtained for every transfer in the chain of title.
items.why: Under the Land Use Act 1978, an alienation without Governor's Consent is void.

items.task: Confirm the seller's identity matches the name on the title document (ID check: BVN, NIN, international passport).
items.why: Impersonation of a true owner is a common fraud vector.

items.task: Where the seller is a company, obtain certified copies of its CAC registration, its board resolution authorising the sale, and confirm directors' identities.
items.why: Unauthorised corporate sellers are a known risk in commercial land transactions.

categories.title: Official Searches
categories.note: TODO-REVIEW: Search procedures and fees change periodically. Confirm current process.

items.task: Conduct an official search at the Lagos State Land Bureau, Alausa, Ikeja.
items.why: Reveals encumbrances, government schemes, court orders, or adverse interests registered on the title.

items.task: Search the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) if the seller or any party in the chain is a company.
items.why: Confirms company existence, directors, and that the company is not under receivership or winding-up.

items.task: Check the Federal High Court and Lagos State High Court cause lists / judgment registers for any litigation concerning the property.
items.why: Active or pending litigation can result in the land being frozen or ownership reversed.

items.task: Obtain a search result from the Lagos State Ministry of Physical Planning and Urban Development to confirm the land is not earmarked for road alignment, public use, or infrastructure.
items.why: Government infrastructure schemes can extinguish private rights without adequate compensation.

items.task: Engage a SURCON-registered surveyor to prepare or authenticate the survey plan.
items.why: Only registered surveyors may legally prepare survey plans in Nigeria.

items.task: Cross-check the survey plan coordinates against satellite imagery and physical beacons on site.
items.why: Sellers sometimes present plans for a different parcel than the one being shown.

items.task: Confirm the land does not fall within a global acquisition area, committed government scheme, or buffer zone (e.g. pipeline, power line easement, waterway).
items.why: Land within such zones cannot be privately owned or developed.

items.task: Visit the land at different times of day, including during rainfall, to assess flooding, drainage, and environmental conditions.
items.why: Many Lagos parcels are prone to flooding. This is not disclosed in title documents.

items.task: Ask the seller to confirm in writing that the property is free of mortgages, liens, or charges.
items.why: A mortgaged property may be repossessed by the lender regardless of your purchase.

items.task: Inspect the property for evidence of third-party occupation: tenants, family members, or community occupants.
items.why: Occupants may have cognisable rights that survive a sale.

items.task: Where family land is involved, obtain evidence that all principal family members or the head of family has consented to the sale.
items.why: Sales by one member of a family without family consent are frequently litigated and reversed.

items.task: Make all payments by traceable bank transfer to the account of the documented owner (not an agent or third party).
items.why: Cash payments are untraceably lost if the transaction is later challenged.

items.task: Do not release final payment until all original title documents are handed over and you have taken physical possession.
items.why: Sellers who receive full payment have little incentive to complete post-completion obligations.

items.task: Budget for all government fees: stamp duty, Land Registry registration fees, Governor's Consent fees, and surveyor fees, in addition to the purchase price.
items.why: These costs can add 10–20% to the headline price depending on the transaction value. TODO-REVIEW: Fee percentages change; confirm current rates.
